blocks.content: The Docker client is the docker command you type into your terminal. It does almost no work itself, it is a thin translator that turns your commands into API requests and hands them off to something else entirely: the Docker daemon.

When you run docker ps, the client does not go look up running containers itself. It builds a REST API request that means "list running containers," sends it off, and waits for a response to print. Think of the client like a restaurant waiter: it takes your order and carries it to the kitchen, it does not cook the food.

blocks.alt: The client turns your command into an API call

blocks.content: 2. How the Client Reaches the Daemon: a Socket
blocks.text: 2. How the Client Reaches the Daemon: a Socket

blocks.content: On a typical local setup, the client talks to the daemon over a Unix socket at /var/run/docker.sock. This is why, on Linux, adding your user to the docker group (rather than needing sudo every time) is really about permission to read and write that one socket file.

blocks.alt: A local socket file is the usual client-daemon bridge

blocks.content:
docker version
# The output has two sections: "Client" and "Server".
# They can even be different versions, since they are separate programs.

blocks.content: 3. The Client Can Also Talk to a Remote Daemon
blocks.text: 3. The Client Can Also Talk to a Remote Daemon

blocks.content: The client is not tied to a daemon on the same machine. Setting the DOCKER_HOST environment variable (or using docker context) points the same client at a daemon running on a different server entirely, over TCP, usually secured with TLS certificates.

blocks.alt: One client, pointed at a daemon somewhere else entirely

blocks.content:
export DOCKER_HOST="tcp://203.0.113.10:2376"
docker ps
# Lists containers running on the remote host, not your local machine.

blocks.content: 4. Every Command Goes Through the Same Client
blocks.text: 4. Every Command Goes Through the Same Client

blocks.content: Whether you are building an image, starting a container, or tailing logs, it is the same client binary underneath, just formatting a different API call each time.

blocks.alt: One CLI, many commands, all shaped into API calls

blocks.content: Nothing stops several different clients from talking to the same daemon at once: your terminal, Docker Desktop's graphical interface, and a CI runner can all issue commands against the same underlying daemon, because the daemon has no idea (or care) which kind of client sent a request.

blocks.alt: The daemon does not care which client is asking

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The docker CLI is a thin client. It translates your commands into REST API calls and sends them to the daemon, which does the actual work.
The client-daemon split is what lets the same client manage a local daemon or a completely remote one, just by changing where it connects.
